NEW POST OFFICE READY FOR CHRISTMAS.

London's new letter-sorting office at Mount Pleasant is now fully equipped to deal with the heavy mail% that always taxes the resources of the Post Office at Xmas. Equipped with electric conveyors and mail-bag laundry, it can deal with 18,000,000 letters weekly. The building which is quite up to date in all its equipment cost £700,000.

SAVAJE WARFARE.
English Officers Learn Principles of Hill Fighting from Major of Gurkhas.
(FROM OUR SPECIAL CORRESPONDENT.)

LLANBERIS, Monday.—The War Office experiment of training officers in mountain warfare was commenced to-day at Llanberis, under the direction of Major Bruce, of the 5th Gurkhas, and Colonel Hoskins, of the Staff College.

The general idea of to-day's work was that Snowdonia was in the hands of a savage enemy, and that three columns of British troops, each 4,000 strong, had arrived overnight and were encamped in the Pass of Llanberis.

These imaginary columns would advance by separate routes to drive the enemy from the mountainous country around Llanberis, and to-day Major Bruce and the party took the line of route which the centre imaginary column would take.

Scouts are supposed to have climbed the nearer hills in the dead of night, and to have located the enemy, the column starting at dawn. The main body would extend in single file a length of ten miles, with mule transport and food for a week.
The whole campaign was gone through in imagination by the party. They are all young and, fresh from the hard training of the manoeuvres, appeared very fit.

Major Bruce set a hot pace, fortunately with intervals for short lectures, brief halts which were welcome to some at least; but the major found no need to pause for breath before plunging into his lecturete.
He is a noted mountaineer, and I am told by a sergeant who served under him that he is known in India as the King of the Gurkhas, and that he can do as much on the hills as the Gurkhas themselves.

His boots were made in India, and have rope soles studded with huge Pathan nails. The twenty-eight officers were dressed in walking suits, and two or three wore shorts. One in particular who showed rather much knee was dubbed "the boy scout," to the general amusement.
From their headquarters at Pen-y-Gwryd the party will start each day and work out some fresh phase of mountain warfare for the fortnight over which the experiment extends.

I read with great interest the letter of "Single of Necessity" in your Monday's issue. I am sure no one for an instant would imagine that he is selfish in remaining single; creatures of his ideas are better so.

I would remind him that modern books can be obtained from free and circulating libraries; that it is quite possible for a woman to do, and not be ashamed of doing, her own housework; to dress on a few shillings a month, and at the same time be well enough educated and refined to be a fit companion for the most fastidious and intellectual specimen of the male species, although there certainly could be no sympathy between her and the holder of such snoblish ideas.

Both "A Mere Woman" and "Secretary" seem to think that woman's main idea is to have a home of her own, however humble, if only she can find a husband to provide it. An ideal state of affairs in anticipation, but many clever, thoughtful women of to-day prefer to remain single and earn their own livelihood rather than experience this "bliss" in reality. On the other hand, no honourable, sensible man expects a reasonable woman to change her lot "for worse."

October 20.-The first week in November is probably the best time for the planting of roses. The growths are then ripe, and, as the soil still retains some of the summer's heat, new roots will form before winter weather arrives. Beds intended for roses must be prepared without delay, otherwise the soil will not have time to settle down. Let the ground be dug as deeply as possible and made fairly rich. Sites for roses against walls should be well prepared if the plants are to do well.

Now that we have so many lovely hambling roses the "queen of flowers" may be seen decking banks, trees, hedges, fences and other suitable positions. For the next few days I will go over the various classes into which roses are divided, naming the best sorts that the small grower ought to cultivate. E. F. T.
